title: CSRF — Cross-Site Request Forgery
subtitle: How attackers trick browsers into making authenticated requests — and why SameSite cookies are the modern defence

content.text: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) exploits the browser's behaviour of automatically attaching cookies to every request to a domain — even requests initiated from a different site. If a user is logged into bank.com and visits evil.com, a hidden form on evil.com can submit a request to bank.com that the browser sends with the user's session cookie. The bank sees a legitimate-looking request with valid credentials and processes it.

content.code:
<!-- The attacker hosts this on evil.com -->
<!-- User is logged into bank.com in another tab -->

<!-- Visible attack (with social engineering): -->
<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="10000" />
  <input type="hidden" name="to_account" value="attacker_account" />
  <button>Click to claim your prize!</button>
</form>

<!-- Silent attack (auto-submits on page load): -->
<form id="csrf" action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST" style="display:none">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="10000" />
  <input type="hidden" name="to_account" value="attacker_account" />
</form>
<script>document.getElementById('csrf').submit();</script>

<!-- The browser sends the request to bank.com WITH the user's session cookie -->
<!-- bank.com sees: authenticated user, valid session, transfer request -->
<!-- bank.com processes the transfer -->
<!-- The user never knew -->

content.text: Defence 2 — CSRF tokens (older apps, still widely used)

For new apps: SameSite=Lax on session cookies is sufficient CSRF protection. All modern browsers (Chrome 80+, Firefox 79+, Safari 13+) default to SameSite=Lax even if you don't set it explicitly. CSRF tokens are still recommended for defense-in-depth and for apps that need to support older browsers or use SameSite=None. For JSON APIs that only accept Content-Type: application/json — a cross-site form can't set that header — CSRF is not a concern for those endpoints.

questions.question: Your API only accepts requests with Content-Type: application/json. Can a CSRF attack still work?
options: Yes — an attacker can set any header from evil.com
No — a cross-site HTML form cannot set Content-Type: application/json, so a valid attack request is impossible to craft without JavaScript fetch(), which is blocked by CORS
Yes — but only on mobile browsers
No — JSON requests are inherently CSRF-safe
questions.explanation: An HTML form can only send application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain. It cannot send application/json. So a form-based CSRF attack against a JSON-only endpoint fails. An attacker could try using JavaScript fetch() with application/json, but cross-site fetch() is subject to CORS preflight — if your CORS policy doesn't allow the attacker's origin, the browser blocks it before the request reaches the server. This combination (Content-Type: application/json + restrictive CORS) provides solid CSRF protection for SPAs, but SameSite cookies are simpler and should still be set.

faq.a: CSRF can technically affect GET requests if they perform state changes (bad practice). An attacker can include an tag — the browser GETs the URL with cookies. This is why state-changing actions should NEVER use GET. The HTTP standard says GET should be idempotent (reading data, not changing it). Restrict CSRF defences to POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE — but also fix any GET endpoints that change state.

examples: In 2008, a CSRF vulnerability in a popular home router's admin interface let attackers change DNS settings by embedding a hidden request in a webpage. Users who visited the malicious page while logged into their router had their DNS silently redirected to attacker-controlled servers — all web traffic intercepted without any sign-in

Django and Rails have built-in CSRF protection that's enabled by default. It's one reason full-stack frameworks are safer out of the box than building from scratch. The CSRF middleware validates a token on every POST — a feature that caught countless vulnerabilities before developers even knew to look for them
